title: How would you partition a database that has outgrown one node?
description: Learn to choose between vertical and horizontal partitioning, evaluate sharding strategies, and explain the operational trade-offs of splitting a database across multiple nodes.

data.text: A single database node eventually runs into limits: storage capacity, I/O throughput, or connection limits. Partitioning is the act of splitting that data so multiple machines can share the load. The right strategy depends on your data shape, query patterns, and operational maturity.

Split tables by function rather than by row. Move infrequently accessed columns to a separate table or even a separate database. This is often the first step because it requires minimal application changes.

items: Low risk and reversible compared to sharding
Does not solve scale-out for high-volume tables
Adds joins for queries that need both partitions

data.text: Split rows of the same table across multiple database instances. Each shard holds a subset of the data, and the application or a proxy routes queries to the correct shard.

terms.definition: The column or expression used to assign each row to a shard.
Moving data between shards when one becomes too large or too hot.
The process of changing the sharding scheme, which often requires downtime or a dual-write migration.

data.title: Sharding by tenant ID
data.content: A SaaS application shards by tenant ID. Tenants A-M go to shard 1, N-Z to shard 2. A new tenant lookup service routes queries. When shard 1 reaches capacity, the team splits it by tenant ID ranges, migrating tenants M and earlier to a new shard.

data.title: Critical decision
data.text: You can rarely change the shard key after sharding. Choose carefully—changing it requires massive data migration and application rewrites.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Start with vertical partitioning before horizontal
Choose a shard key with high cardinality and even distribution
Resharding is expensive; plan for growth, not just current load
